title: Drumline
full_review:
A talented but cocky drummer jeopardizes his college scholarship when he wants to be the star of the school band in "Drumline" (20th Century Fox).

Although Dad didn't stick around, Devon (Nick Cannon) grew up in Harlem, kept out of trouble and graduated from high school with a music scholarship to a predominately black university in Atlanta.

A hip-hop drummer with amazing technique, Devon was recruited by the band's director, Dr. Lee (Orlando Jones), and arrives on campus unprepared for the strict discipline that qualifying for the band demands. He bristles when criticized by the drum section leader, Sean (Leonard Roberts), a senior who recognizes his talent but despises his cocky attitude.

Dr. Lee is under pressure by the university president (Afem Omilami) to scrap classical selections in favor of the kind of current music their rival school uses to win in the yearly band competition. When Devon moves in on Sean's solo drum number at one of the football games, the president is impressed with his jazzy playing, but Dr. Lee and Sean realize the freshman needs to be taken down a peg or two and learn the concept of teamwork.

The story is formulaic, but the setting of a college marching band is fresh and the music and dance production numbers keep the interest level up in spite of the predictability factor.

When Devon is pulled from the band, the rival band director (J. Anthony Brown) offers him a cushy spot -- for a price that tests the young man's sense of ethics. And Devon is not the only one who has to learn some hard lessons; Dr. Lee pushes Sean to question if he is hard on Devon for the right reasons, or out of jealousy over the freshman's superior talent.

Zoe Saldana plays Devon's student love interest, Laila, in a supportive relationship that helps both of them mature without suggesting an ongoing steamy affair. There are wisecracks about virginity and comparing playing an instrument to sex but this and the occasional crude word are passing moments in director Charles Stone III's otherwise wholesome, even high-minded, film.

Although the movie feels a little long, its themes of not lying, developing integrity and working toward personal growth are real pluses. And the sturdy appeal of an underdog band taking on the rival-band-that-can't-be-beat at the conclusion sends it into feel-good territory.

Without much fanfare but a sense of humor, toe-tapping numbers and energetic camerawork, "Drumline" has been finding fans at the box office.

Due to a few sexual references and crass expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
